attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own essay.

semantics.note: An unhedged 'will' forecast that the criticised tech companies will be forced to change. Public pressure is the stated mechanism, not a true conditional. There is no deadline.

contract.note: The plain reading (meaningful changes to criticised practices caused by public pressure, not every practice changing) is fair and ordinary. Calling pressure an 'antecedent' is a slight framing issue but changes nothing.

evidence.note: Independent report of user backlash and OpenAI's rollback of the sycophantic update. This is one instance about a practice Zitron did not specifically criticise. It does not establish the collective pattern.
Company disclosure confirming the rollback. One product correction, which the contract says is insufficient on its own.
Google removed some health AI Overviews after the Guardian's reporting, but others persisted. A limited response that neither establishes nor rules out the forecast.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm forecast with no deadline. The packet shows two isolated, partial responses to criticism, which falls short of the collective pattern of change the forecast predicts. No event makes the outcome impossible, and with no deadline, elapsed time cannot count as failure. Unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own essay.

semantics.note: A compound present-tense observation about the generative AI industry: over-leverage, no real path to profitability, burning billions, and environmental harm. The normalisation drops the causal framing of 'the result' of short-termism but otherwise matches.

contract.note: The evaluator chose the target quarter (Q3 2024) and the net-cash metric because the speaker named none. That is a reasonable ordinary reading, but it determines what evidence counts. 'No real path to profitability' is partly a judgment.

evidence.note: A full-year 2024 loss projection for one company (OpenAI). It is a different period from the target quarter and not an industry total.
OpenAI's credit line was undrawn at closing in October 2024. One company, after the target period. It does not settle industry leverage.
Research on the energy use of AI inference. It gives no aggregate harm figure for the target period and says nothing on information pollution.

reviews.rationale: The packet has single-company figures for other periods and general energy research. None of it establishes or refutes industry-wide leverage, billion-dollar net cash burn in the target quarter, the absence of a profitability route, or environmental harm. The compound claim stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words. Although framed as 'be the person who tells people', he plainly endorses the content.

semantics.note: The normalisation correctly isolates the creative-works part of a compound sentence and renders 'larceny' as 'theft'. The financial, environmental and motive parts are excluded.

contract.note: Reading 'larceny' as substantial unauthorised copying, including pirated copies, rather than a criminal conviction is the ordinary reading of this rhetoric. Keeping the fair-use question separate is fair.

evidence.note: The court order records as undisputed that an OpenAI employee downloaded pirated LibGen books in 2018. The link to the Books datasets is a plaintiffs' assertion. It is a discovery ruling, not a merits ruling.
Plaintiffs' filing quotes an internal 2019 OpenAI note saying GPT-3 was trained on pirated material. It is an OpenAI document presented by an adverse party.
Plaintiffs' statement of facts, citing depositions, puts the LibGen download at about 117,859 books. This supports large scale, though the count is the plaintiffs' presentation.
OpenAI argues training is fair use. That disputes the legal characterisation but does not deny unlicensed use.

reviews.rationale: The court records an undisputed pirated LibGen download. An internal OpenAI note quoted in the filing ties pirated material to GPT-3 training, and deposition-backed facts put the download at over 100,000 books, all before the post. That meets the contract's unauthorised-use reading. The fair-use question remains open in court and is outside the claim.
